modules.content:
===== PDF PAGE 344 =====
●  Deposit  validation  ●  Withdrawal  validation  ●  No  negative  balance  ●  @property to  read  balance  ●  Proper  exception  handling  
🐍  Module  14:  Inheritance  in  Python  
So  far:  
Module  12  →  Classes  &  Objects  Module  13  →  Encapsulation  Module  14  →  🔥  Inheritance  
The  main  idea  is:  
Inheritance  allows  one  class  to  reuse  and  extend  the  properties  and  
methods
 
of
 
another
 
class.
 
 
14.1  What  is  Inheritance?  
Suppose  we  have:  
class  Animal:      def  eat(self):          print("Animal  is  eating")  
Now  we  create:  
class  Dog(Animal):      pass  
Dog inherits  from  Animal.  
So:  
dog  =  Dog()   dog.eat()  
Output:  
Animal  is  eating

===== PDF PAGE 345 =====
The  Dog class  didn't  define  eat(),  but  it  can  use  the  method  from  Animal.  
 
14.2  Parent  and  Child  Class  
In:  
class  Dog(Animal):  
we  have:  
Animal  →  Parent  class  /  Base  class  /  Superclass   Dog  →  Child  class  /  Derived  class  /  Subclass  
Easy  memory:  
Parent    ↓  Child    ↓  Gets/reuses  functionality   
14.3  Why  Use  Inheritance?  
Imagine  we  have:  
Animal   ├──  name   ├──  age   ├──  eat()   └──  sleep()  
Then:  
Dog   ├──  bark()   └──  inherited  eat(),  sleep()   Cat   ├──  meow()   └──  inherited  eat(),  sleep()  
We  don't  need  to  write  eat() and  sleep() repeatedly.

===== PDF PAGE 346 =====
Benefits  Inheritance      ↓  Code  reuse      ↓  Less  duplication      ↓  Better  organization      ↓  Easy  extension   
14.4  Basic  Syntax  
class  Parent:      #  parent  members    class  Child(Parent):      #  child  members  
Example:  
class  Animal:       def  eat(self):          print("Eating")    class  Dog(Animal):       def  bark(self):          print("Barking")  
Use:  
dog  =  Dog()   dog.eat()  dog.bark()  
Output:  
Eating  Barking

===== PDF PAGE 347 =====
14.5  Inheritance  Flowchart  
            Animal            Parent  Class                 │         ┌───────┴────────┐         ↓                 ↓        Dog               Cat     Child  Class       Child  Class         │                 │      bark()             meow()         │                 │         └────  inherited  ─┘            eat(),  sleep()   
14.6  Parent  Constructor  
Consider:  
class  Person:       def  __init__(self,  name):          self.name  =  name  
Child:  
class  Student(Person):      pass  
Now:  
student  =  Student("Prasanna")   print(student.name)  
Output:  
Prasanna  
The  child  can  use  the  inherited  constructor.  
 
14.7  Child  with  Its  Own  Constructor

===== PDF PAGE 348 =====
Suppose:  
class  Person:       def  __init__(self,  name):          self.name  =  name    class  Student(Person):       def  __init__(self,  name,  marks):          self.name  =  name          self.marks  =  marks  
Now:  
student  =  Student("Prasanna",  90)  
The  child's  __init__() replaces  the  inherited  constructor  for  Student.  
But  there's  a  better  way  when  we  want  to  reuse  the  parent's  initialization.  
 
14.8  super() ⭐⭐⭐  
super() is  used  to  access  functionality  from  the  parent  class.  
Example:  
class  Person:       def  __init__(self,  name):          self.name  =  name    class  Student(Person):       def  __init__(self,  name,  marks):          super().__init__(name)          self.marks  =  marks  
Now:  
student  =  Student("Prasanna",  90)   print(student.name)

===== PDF PAGE 349 =====
print(student.marks)  
Output:  
Prasanna  90   
14.9  Understanding  super()  
Without  super():  
self.name  =  name  
has  to  be  repeated  in  the  child.  
With:  
super().__init__(name)  
we  tell  Python:  
"Run  the  parent  class's  initialization  logic."  
Flow:  
Student(...)       ↓  Student.__init__()       ↓  super().__init__()       ↓  Person.__init__()       ↓  self.name  =  name       ↓  Back  to  Student       ↓  self.marks  =  marks   
14.10  Why  super() Is  Useful  
Suppose  parent  has:  
class  Person:

===== PDF PAGE 350 =====
def  __init__(self,  name,  age):          self.name  =  name          self.age  =  age  
Child:  
class  Student(Person):       def  __init__(self,  name,  age,  marks):          super().__init__(name,  age)          self.marks  =  marks  
Now  parent  handles:  
name  age  
and  child  handles:  
marks  
This  avoids  duplicate  code.  
 
14.11  Method  Inheritance  
Parent:  
class  Animal:       def  eat(self):          print("Eating")  
Child:  
class  Dog(Animal):      pass  
Then:  
dog  =  Dog()   dog.eat()  
Output:  
Eating

===== PDF PAGE 351 =====
14.12  Adding  New  Methods  
Child  classes  can  add  their  own  behavior.  
class  Animal:       def  eat(self):          print("Eating")    class  Dog(Animal):       def  bark(self):          print("Barking")  
Now:  
dog  =  Dog()   dog.eat()  dog.bark()  
Output:  
Eating  Barking  
So  inheritance  doesn't  mean  the  child  can  only  use  parent  functionality.  
It  can  also  add  new  functionality.  
 
14.13  Method  Overriding  ⭐⭐⭐  
Suppose  the  parent  has:  
class  Animal:       def  sound(self):          print("Animal  makes  a  sound")  
Child  defines  a  method  with  the  same  name:

===== PDF PAGE 352 =====
class  Dog(Animal):       def  sound(self):          print("Dog  barks")  
Now:  
dog  =  Dog()   dog.sound()  
Output:  
Dog  barks  
The  child's  method  overrides  the  parent's  method  for  Dog objects.  
 
14.14  What  Is  Method  Overriding?  
When  a  child  class  provides  its  own  implementation  of  a  method  inherited  from  
the
 
parent,
 
that
 
is
 
method
 
overriding.
 
Flow:  
Parent    ↓  sound()    ↓  Child    ↓  sound()  again    ↓  Child  implementation  used   
14.15  Calling  the  Parent's  Overridden  
Method
 
Sometimes  we  want  both  the  child  and  parent  behavior.  
Use:  
super()

===== PDF PAGE 353 =====
Example:  
class  Animal:       def  sound(self):          print("Animal  makes  a  sound")    class  Dog(Animal):       def  sound(self):          super().sound()          print("Dog  barks")  
Now:  
dog  =  Dog()   dog.sound()  
Output:  
Animal  makes  a  sound  Dog  barks   
14.16  Real-Life  Example:  Employee  
Parent:  
class  Employee:       def  __init__(self,  name,  salary):          self.name  =  name          self.salary  =  salary       def  display(self):          print("Name:",  self.name)          print("Salary:",  self.salary)  
Child:  
class  Manager(Employee):       def  __init__(self,  name,  salary,  team_size):          super().__init__(name,  salary)          self.team_size  =  team_size

===== PDF PAGE 354 =====
Use:  
manager  =  Manager("Prasanna",  60000,  10)   manager.display()  print("Team:",  manager.team_size)  
Output:  
Name:  Prasanna  Salary:  60000  Team:  10   
14.17  Types  of  Inheritance  ⭐⭐⭐  
Python  supports  several  inheritance  patterns:  
1.  Single  Inheritance  2.  Multiple  Inheritance  3.  Multilevel  Inheritance  4.  Hierarchical  Inheritance  5.  Hybrid  Inheritance  
Let's  understand  them  one  by  one.  
 
14.18  Single  Inheritance  
One  parent  →  one  child.  
Animal     ↓   Dog  
Code:  
class  Animal:       def  eat(self):          print("Eating")    class  Dog(Animal):

===== PDF PAGE 355 =====
def  bark(self):          print("Barking")  
This  is  single  inheritance .  
 
14.19  Multiple  Inheritance  
One  child  inherits  from  multiple  parents.  
Parent1        Parent2      \            /       \          /         Child  
Example:  
class  Father:       def  skills(self):          print("Driving")    class  Mother:       def  talent(self):          print("Cooking")    class  Child(Father,  Mother):      pass  
Now:  
child  =  Child()   child.skills()  child.talent()  
Output:  
Driving  Cooking  
The  child  inherits  from  both  classes.

===== PDF PAGE 356 =====
14.20  Multiple  Inheritance  Example  
class  Camera:       def  take_photo(self):          print("Taking  photo")    class  Phone:       def  make_call(self):          print("Making  call")    class  Smartphone(Camera,  Phone):      pass  
Now:  
phone  =  Smartphone()   phone.take_photo()  phone.make_call()  
Output:  
Taking  photo  Making  call   
14.21  Multilevel  Inheritance  
Inheritance  happens  across  multiple  levels.  
Grandparent       ↓     Parent       ↓     Child  
Example:  
class  Animal:       def  eat(self):          print("Eating")

===== PDF PAGE 357 =====
class  Dog(Animal):       def  bark(self):          print("Barking")    class  Puppy(Dog):       def  play(self):          print("Playing")  
Now:  
puppy  =  Puppy()   puppy.eat()  puppy.bark()  puppy.play()  
Output:  
Eating  Barking  Playing   
14.22  Hierarchical  Inheritance  
One  parent  →  multiple  children.  
         Animal           /       \          ↓         ↓        Dog        Cat  
Code:  
class  Animal:       def  eat(self):          print("Eating")    class  Dog(Animal):       def  bark(self):

===== PDF PAGE 358 =====
print("Barking")    class  Cat(Animal):       def  meow(self):          print("Meowing")  
Both  can  use:  
animal.eat()  
through  inheritance.  
 
14.23  Hybrid  Inheritance  
Hybrid  inheritance  is  a  combination  of  multiple  inheritance  patterns.  
For  example:  
         A           /  \          B    C           \  /            D  
This  combines  hierarchical  and  multiple  inheritance.  
Python  can  support  such  structures,  but  they  should  be  designed  carefully.  
 
14.24  Method  Resolution  Order  —  MRO  
⭐⭐⭐
 
MRO  determines  the  order  in  which  Python  searches  classes  for  methods  and  attributes.  
Example:  
class  A:      def  show(self):          print("A")

===== PDF PAGE 359 =====
class  B(A):      def  show(self):          print("B")    class  C(B):      pass  
Calling:  
c  =  C()  c.show()  
Python  searches:  
C  ↓  B  ↓  A  ↓  object  
So  output:  
B   
14.25  Checking  MRO  
Use:  
print(C.mro())  
or:  
print(C.__mro__)  
You'll  see  a  sequence  containing  something  like:  
C  →  B  →  A  →  object  
This  is  extremely  important  for  understanding  multiple  inheritance.

===== PDF PAGE 360 =====
14.26  object Class  
In  Python,  normal  classes  ultimately  derive  from:  
object  
Conceptually:  
YourClass     ↓  object  
That's  why:  
class  Student:      pass  
is  effectively  a  subclass  of  object.  
 
14.27  Diamond  Problem  ⭐⭐⭐  
Consider:  
      A        /  \       B    C        \  /         D  
D inherits  from  both  B and  C.  
The  question  is:  
If  B  and  C  both  inherit  from  A,  which  version  should  Python  use?  
Python  solves  this  using  Method  Resolution  Order  (MRO)  and  the  C3  linearization  
algorithm
.
 
Example:  
class  A:      def  show(self):          print("A")

===== PDF PAGE 361 =====
class  B(A):      def  show(self):          print("B")    class  C(A):      def  show(self):          print("C")    class  D(B,  C):      pass  
Then:  
d  =  D()   d.show()  
Output:  
B  
Because  MRO  starts  with:  
D  →  B  →  C  →  A  →  object   
14.28  super() in  Multiple  Inheritance  
This  is  an  advanced  but  important  idea.  
super() does  not  simply  mean  "my  immediate  parent."  
It  means:  
Continue  method  lookup  according  to  the  class's  MRO.  
Example:  
class  A:       def  show(self):          print("A")    class  B(A):

===== PDF PAGE 362 =====
def  show(self):          print("B")          super().show()    class  C(A):       def  show(self):          print("C")          super().show()    class  D(B,  C):      pass  
Now:  
d  =  D()  d.show()  
Output:  
B  C  A  
Why?  
MRO:  
D  →  B  →  C  →  A  →  object  
super() follows  that  cooperative  MRO.  
This  becomes  especially  useful  in  carefully  designed  multiple-inheritance  systems.  
 
14.29  isinstance() ⭐⭐⭐  
isinstance() checks  whether  an  object  is  an  instance  of  a  class  or  its  subclasses.  
Example:  
class  Animal:      pass

===== PDF PAGE 363 =====
class  Dog(Animal):      pass    dog  =  Dog()   print(isinstance(dog,  Dog))  print(isinstance(dog,  Animal))  
Output:  
True  True  
Because  a  Dog is  also  an  Animal.  
 
14.30  issubclass()  
issubclass() checks  class  relationships.  
class  Animal:      pass    class  Dog(Animal):      pass    print(issubclass(Dog,  Animal))  
Output:  
True   
14.31  Inheritance  vs  Composition  
⭐⭐⭐
 
This  is  an  important  design  concept.  
Inheritance  IS-A  relationship

===== PDF PAGE 364 =====
Example:  
Dog  IS-A  Animal  class  Dog(Animal):      ...  
Composition  HAS-A  relationship  
Example:  
Car  HAS-A  Engine  class  Car:       def  __init__(self):          self.engine  =  Engine()  
A  useful  rule:  
Use  inheritance  when  the  child  truly  represents  a  specialized  form  of  the  parent.  
Use
 
composition
 
when
 
one
 
object
 
contains
 
or
 
uses
 
another
 
object.
 
 
14.32  Real-Life  Composition  Example  
class  Engine:       def  start(self):          print("Engine  started")    class  Car:       def  __init__(self):          self.engine  =  Engine()       def  start(self):          self.engine.start()          print("Car  started")  
Here:  
Car   ↓  HAS-A   ↓

===== PDF PAGE 365 =====
Engine  
This  is  not  inheritance.  
 
14.33  Inheritance  +  Encapsulation  
We  can  combine  Module  13  and  Module  14.  
class  BankAccount:       def  __init__(self,  balance):          self.__balance  =  balance       def  get_balance(self):          return  self.__balance    class  SavingsAccount(BankAccount):       def  add_interest(self,  amount):          #  controlled  public  behavior          print("Interest  added:",  amount)  
SavingsAccount inherits  from  BankAccount.  
 
14.34  Practical  Program:  Vehicle  System  
class  Vehicle:       def  __init__(self,  brand):          self.brand  =  brand       def  start(self):          print(self.brand,  "started")    class  Car(Vehicle):       def  drive(self):          print(self.brand,  "is  driving")

===== PDF PAGE 366 =====
class  Bike(Vehicle):       def  ride(self):          print(self.brand,  "is  riding")  
Use:  
car  =  Car("Toyota")  bike  =  Bike("Yamaha")   car.start()  car.drive()   bike.start()  bike.ride()  
Output:  
Toyota  started  Toyota  is  driving  Yamaha  started  Yamaha  is  riding   
14.35  Practical  Program:  Student  
Hierarchy
 
class  Person:       def  __init__(self,  name,  age):          self.name  =  name          self.age  =  age    class  Student(Person):       def  __init__(self,  name,  age,  roll_no):          super().__init__(name,  age)          self.roll_no  =  roll_no       def  display(self):          print("Name:",  self.name)          print("Age:",  self.age)          print("Roll  No:",  self.roll_no)  
Use:

===== PDF PAGE 367 =====
student  =  Student("Prasanna",  20,  101)   student.display()  
Output:  
Name:  Prasanna  Age:  20  Roll  No:  101   
14.36  Practical  Program:  Employee  
Hierarchy
 
class  Employee:       def  __init__(self,  name,  salary):          self.name  =  name          self.salary  =  salary       def  display(self):          print("Name:",  self.name)          print("Salary:",  self.salary)    class  Developer(Employee):       def  code(self):          print(self.name,  "is  coding")    class  Manager(Employee):       def  manage(self):          print(self.name,  "is  managing")  
Use:  
developer  =  Developer("Prasanna",  50000)  manager  =  Manager("Ravi",  70000)   developer.display()  developer.code()   manager.display()  manager.manage()

===== PDF PAGE 368 =====
14.37  Module  14  Flowchart  
                   INHERITANCE                           ↓                    Parent  Class                           ↓                   ┌───────┴───────┐                   ↓                ↓               Child  Class      Child  Class                   ↓                ↓               New  methods      New  methods                   │                │                   └───────┬───────┘                           ↓                     Code  Reuse  
With  overriding:  
Parent  method        ↓  Child  defines  same  method        ↓  Child  implementation  used  
With  super():  
Child  method       ↓  super()       ↓  Parent/MRO  implementation   
14.38  Types  of  Inheritance  —  Quick  
Revision
 
1.  Single   A  ↓  B

===== PDF PAGE 369 =====
2.  Multiple   A      B   \    /     C    3.  Multilevel   A  ↓  B  ↓  C    4.  Hierarchical       A     /  \    B    C    5.  Hybrid   Combination  of  inheritance  patterns   
14.39  Important  Interview  Questions  
⭐⭐⭐
 
Q1.  What  is  inheritance?  
Inheritance  allows  a  child  class  to  reuse  and  extend  functionality  from  a  parent  class.  
Q2.  Why  use  inheritance?  
For:  
●  Code  reuse  ●  Specialization  ●  Reduced  duplication  ●  Extending  existing  behavior  
Q3.  What  is  super()?

===== PDF PAGE 370 =====
It  provides  a  way  to  delegate  method/attribute  lookup  to  the  next  class  in  the  MRO.  
Q4.  What  is  method  overriding?  
When  a  child  class  provides  its  own  implementation  of  an  inherited  method.  
Q5.  What  are  the  types  of  inheritance?  Single  Multiple  Multilevel  Hierarchical  Hybrid  
Q6.  What  is  MRO?  
Method  Resolution  Order  —  the  order  Python  follows  when  searching  classes  for  methods  
and
 
attributes.
 
Q7.  How  do  you  check  MRO?  ClassName.mro()  
or:  
ClassName.__mro__  
Q8.  What  is  the  diamond  problem?  
It  occurs  in  certain  multiple-inheritance  structures  where  a  class  inherits  through  multiple  
paths
 
from
 
the
 
same
 
ancestor.
 
Python
 
resolves
 
the
 
lookup
 
order
 
using
 
MRO/C3
 
linearization.
 
Q9.  What  is  isinstance()?  
Checks  whether  an  object  is  an  instance  of  a  class  or  its  subclasses.  
Q10.  What  is  issubclass()?  
Checks  whether  one  class  is  a  subclass  of  another.  
 
14.40  Most  Important  Difference  
Inheritance  IS-A

===== PDF PAGE 371 =====
Example:  
Dog  IS-A  Animal  
Composition  HAS-A  
Example:  
Car  HAS-A  Engine  
This  distinction  is  important  when  designing  real-world  applications.

Parent  constructor  super().__init__(...)

modules.title: Polymorphism in Python
modules.content:
===== PDF PAGE 373 =====
🔥  Challenge  
Build  a  College  Management  System :  
                   Person                     /       \                    /         \               Student       Employee                  │             │               Graduate       Teacher  
Requirements:  
Person  name  age  display()  
Student  roll_no  marks  result()  
GraduateStudent  specialization  
Employee  employee_id  salary  
Teacher  subject  teach()  
Use:  
Inheritance  +  super()  +  Method  overriding  
🐍  Module  15:  Polymorphism  in  Python

===== PDF PAGE 374 =====
Our  OOP  journey:  
Module  12  →  Classes  &  Objects  Module  13  →  Encapsulation  Module  14  →  Inheritance  Module  15  →  🔥  Polymorphism  Module  16  →  Abstraction   
15.1  What  is  Polymorphism?  
Polymorphism  means:  
One  interface,  many  forms.  
The  same  method  name  or  operation  can  behave  differently  depending  on  the  object  
involved.
 
The  word  comes  from:  
Poly  →  Many  Morph  →  Forms  
So:  
Polymorphism       ↓  One  interface       ↓  Different  behavior   
15.2  Real-Life  Example  
Think  about  the  action:  
"Speak"  
Different  animals  speak  differently:  
Dog  →  Bark  Cat  →  Meow  Cow  →  Moo  
But  we  can  use  the  same  method:  
animal.speak()

===== PDF PAGE 375 =====
The  behavior  depends  on  the  object.  
 
15.3  Simple  Example  
class  Dog:       def  sound(self):          print("Bark")    class  Cat:       def  sound(self):          print("Meow")  
Now:  
dog  =  Dog()  cat  =  Cat()   dog.sound()  cat.sound()  
Output:  
Bark  Meow  
Same  method  name:  
sound()  
Different  behavior:  
Dog  →  Bark  Cat  →  Meow  
That's  polymorphism.  
 
15.4  Polymorphism  Flowchart  
                sound()                      ↓

===== PDF PAGE 376 =====
┌─────────┴─────────┐            ↓                    ↓          Dog                   Cat            ↓                    ↓         Bark                   Meow   
15.5  Polymorphism  with  Inheritance  
⭐⭐⭐
 
Polymorphism  is  commonly  used  together  with  inheritance.  
Parent:  
class  Animal:       def  sound(self):          print("Animal  sound")  
Children:  
class  Dog(Animal):       def  sound(self):          print("Bark")    class  Cat(Animal):       def  sound(self):          print("Meow")  
Now:  
dog  =  Dog()  cat  =  Cat()   dog.sound()  cat.sound()  
Output:  
Bark  Meow  
The  child  classes  override  the  parent  method.

===== PDF PAGE 377 =====
15.6  Method  Overriding  
This  is  one  of  the  most  common  forms  of  polymorphism  in  Python.  
Parent:  
class  Animal:       def  sound(self):          print("Animal  sound")  
Child:  
class  Dog(Animal):       def  sound(self):          print("Bark")  
The  child  changes  the  behavior  of  the  inherited  method.  
Parent    ↓  sound()    ↓  Child  overrides    ↓  Different  behavior   
15.7  Same  Method,  Different  Objects  
class  Dog:       def  sound(self):          print("Bark")    class  Cat:       def  sound(self):          print("Meow")    animals  =  [Dog(),  Cat()]

===== PDF PAGE 378 =====
for  animal  in  animals:      animal.sound()  
Output:  
Bark  Meow  
This  is  a  very  important  example.  
We  don't  need:  
if  isinstance(animal,  Dog):      ...  elif  isinstance(animal,  Cat):      ...  
Instead,  we  simply  call:  
animal.sound()  
Each  object  knows  what  sound() means  for  itself.  
 
15.8  Duck  Typing  ⭐⭐⭐  
Python  strongly  supports  a  concept  called  duck  typing .  
The  idea  is:  
If  an  object  behaves  like  what  we  need,  we  can  use  it.  
A  famous  informal  phrase  is:  
"If  it  walks  like  a  duck  and  quacks  like  a  duck,  treat  it  like  a  duck."  
Example:  
class  Dog:       def  speak(self):          print("Bark")    class  Robot:       def  speak(self):

===== PDF PAGE 379 =====
print("Hello")  
Now:  
def  make_it_speak(obj):      obj.speak()  
We  can  call:  
make_it_speak(Dog())  make_it_speak(Robot())  
Output:  
Bark  Hello  
The  function  doesn't  care  whether  the  object  is  a  Dog or  Robot.  
It  only  cares  that  the  object  provides:  
speak()   
15.9  Duck  Typing  Flow  
             make_it_speak(obj)                         ↓                   Does  obj  have                      speak()?                         ↓                  ┌──────┴──────┐                  ↓              ↓                 YES             NO                  ↓              ↓            Call  speak()       Error   
15.10  Why  Duck  Typing  Is  Powerful  
Instead  of  writing:  
if  isinstance(obj,  Dog):      obj.speak()  elif  isinstance(obj,  Cat):      obj.speak()

===== PDF PAGE 380 =====
elif  isinstance(obj,  Robot):      obj.speak()  
we  can  simply:  
obj.speak()  
This  makes  code  more  flexible.  
 
15.11  Polymorphism  with  Functions  
Python  functions  can  work  with  different  object  types.  
def  show_sound(animal):      animal.sound()  
Now:  
show_sound(Dog())  show_sound(Cat())  
Output:  
Bark  Meow  
The  function  doesn't  need  to  know  the  exact  class.  
 
15.12  Polymorphism  with  Built-in  
Functions
 
Python's  built-in  functions  often  work  with  many  types.  
For  example:  
print(len("Python"))  print(len([10,  20,  30]))  
Output:  
6  3

===== PDF PAGE 381 =====
The  same  function:  
len()  
works  with  different  objects.  
This  is  another  example  of  polymorphic  behavior  through  a  common  protocol.  
 
15.13  len() and  __len__()  
When  you  write:  
len(obj)  
Python  can  use  the  object's:  
__len__()  
special  method.  
Example:  
class  Team:       def  __init__(self,  members):          self.members  =  members       def  __len__(self):          return  len(self.members)  
Now:  
team  =  Team(["A",  "B",  "C"])   print(len(team))  
Output:  
3  
This  is  an  example  of  operator/special-method-based  polymorphism .  
 
15.14  Operator  Overloading  ⭐⭐⭐

===== PDF PAGE 382 =====
Python  allows  classes  to  define  how  operators  work  with  their  objects.  
For  example:  
+  -  *  ==  <  >  
can  be  customized  using  special  methods.  
 
15.15  Example:  +  
Normally:  
print(10  +  20)  
Output:  
30  
For  strings:  
print("Hello  "  +  "Python")  
Output:  
Hello  Python  
The  same  operator:  
+  
has  different  behavior  depending  on  the  operands.  
That's  polymorphic  behavior.  
 
15.16  __add__()  
The  + operator  is  associated  with:

===== PDF PAGE 383 =====
__add__()  
Example:  
class  Number:       def  __init__(self,  value):          self.value  =  value       def  __add__(self,  other):          return  Number(self.value  +  other.value)  
Now:  
a  =  Number(10)  b  =  Number(20)   c  =  a  +  b   print(c.value)  
Output:  
30   
15.17  Operator  Overloading  Flow  
a  +  b    ↓  a.__add__(b)    ↓  Custom  implementation    ↓  Result   
15.18  Common  Special  Methods  
Some  useful  special  methods:  
Operator  /  Function  Special  Method  
+ __add__()

===== PDF PAGE 384 =====
- __sub__() 
* __mul__() 
/ __truediv__() 
== __eq__() 
< __lt__() 
> __gt__() 
len() __len__() 
str() __str__() 
These  are  often  called  dunder  methods  because  of  the  double  underscores.  
 
15.19  Dunder  Methods  
"Dunder"  means:  
Double  UNDERscore  
Examples:  
__init__  __str__  __len__  __add__  __eq__  
They  allow  Python's  syntax  and  built-in  functions  to  interact  with  your  objects.  
 
15.20  __eq__() —  Equality  
Suppose:  
class  Student:

===== PDF PAGE 385 =====
def  __init__(self,  name):          self.name  =  name  
Two  objects:  
s1  =  Student("Prasanna")  s2  =  Student("Prasanna")  
By  default:  
print(s1  ==  s2)  
doesn't  automatically  mean  their  names  are  equal.  
We  can  define  equality  ourselves:  
class  Student:       def  __init__(self,  name):          self.name  =  name       def  __eq__(self,  other):          return  self.name  ==  other.name  
Now:  
s1  =  Student("Prasanna")  s2  =  Student("Prasanna")   print(s1  ==  s2)  
Output:  
True   
15.21  __str__() and  Polymorphism  
Recall  Module  12:  
class  Student:       def  __init__(self,  name):          self.name  =  name       def  __str__(self):          return  self.name

===== PDF PAGE 386 =====
Now:  
student  =  Student("Prasanna")   print(student)  
Python  uses:  
student.__str__()  
So  special  methods  let  your  objects  participate  naturally  in  Python  operations.  
 
15.22  Method  Overloading  —  Important  
Python
 
Point
 
⭐⭐⭐
 
In  languages  such  as  Java,  you  can  have  multiple  methods  with  the  same  name  but  different  
parameter
 
lists:
 
add(int,  int)  add(int,  int,  int)  
This  is  called  method  overloading .  
Python  does  not  support  traditional  compile-time  method  overloading  in  that  same  way.  
If  you  define:  
class  Calculator:       def  add(self,  a,  b):          return  a  +  b       def  add(self,  a,  b,  c):          return  a  +  b  +  c  
the  second  add() replaces  the  first  one.  
 
15.23  How  to  Achieve  Flexible  
Arguments
 
in
 
Python

===== PDF PAGE 387 =====
We  can  use  default  arguments:  
class  Calculator:       def  add(self,  a,  b,  c=0):          return  a  +  b  +  c  
Now:  
calc  =  Calculator()   print(calc.add(10,  20))  print(calc.add(10,  20,  30))  
Output:  
30  60   
15.24  Using  *args  
Another  approach:
